# SNAP processing

s1bursts relies on ESA SNAP for the radar processing. This page describes the
steps SNAP applies to a burst, how to inspect them for your own settings, which
SNAP problems s1bursts corrects, and how the supported SNAP versions differ.

## The processing steps

Each product runs through a fixed chain of SNAP operators, called a processing
graph. s1bursts builds the graph from the product's settings object, so the
settings decide which steps run and with which parameters. The default
backscatter graph has eight steps:

| Step | What it does | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| `Apply-Orbit-File` | Replaces the predicted satellite orbit with the precise one | |
| `ThermalNoiseRemoval` | Removes the instrument's own noise | |
| `Calibration` | Converts the raw values to radar brightness | |
| `TOPSAR-Deburst` | Joins the burst into one seamless image | |
| `Multilook` | Averages neighbouring pixels to reduce noise and runtime | `multilook` |
| `Terrain-Flattening` | Corrects brightness for the slope of the terrain | `flatten_terrain` |
| `ReplaceZerosWithNoData` | Marks the empty border of the burst as missing ([why](#corrections-s1bursts-applies)) | `replace_zeros_with_nan` |
| `Terrain-Correction` | Places every pixel on the map, using the DEM | `grid_spacing`, `dem` |

Coherence compares two acquisitions, so its graph differs. Both acquisitions
get precise orbits, then `Back-Geocoding` aligns the second onto the first
pixel by pixel, using the DEM. `Coherence` estimates the similarity of the two
within a moving window, set by `window`, and the last three steps match the
backscatter graph. The interferogram graph replaces `Coherence` with
`Interferogram` and keeps the phase together with each acquisition's
brightness.

## Inspect a graph

Every settings object can show the graph it produces, as a diagram or as the
XML file that SNAP runs. Inspect it to check what your settings change, or to
describe the processing in a publication.

### As a diagram

`to_mermaid()` returns the graph as text in the
[Mermaid](https://mermaid.js.org/) diagram language. In a notebook, the
[mermaid-py](https://github.com/ouhammmourachid/mermaid-py) package draws it.
Install it separately, since s1bursts does not depend on it:

```{.python}
from mermaid import Mermaid
from s1bursts import BackscatterConfig

config = BackscatterConfig(grid_spacing=20)
Mermaid(config.to_mermaid())
```

mermaid-py draws the diagram through the online mermaid.ink service. Without
internet access, paste the text into a `mermaid` code block on GitHub or in
Quarto instead. For the settings above, the graph looks like this:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from s1bursts import BackscatterConfig

config = BackscatterConfig(grid_spacing=20)
print(f"```{{mermaid}}\n{config.to_mermaid().replace('flowchart LR', 'flowchart TD')}\n```")
```

### As XML

`to_xml()` returns the graph in SNAP's own XML format, with every parameter
SNAP receives:

```{python}
xml = config.to_xml()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f':::{{.callout-note collapse="true"}}\n## The full graph\n\n```xml\n{xml}\n```\n:::')
```

The graph leaves two placeholders, `${source}` for the burst file and `${crs}`
for the projection. s1bursts fills them in for every burst it processes, which
is why the projection is passed to the `create_*` methods rather than stored in
the settings. Save the XML beside your results to record exactly how they were
made:

```{.python}
from pathlib import Path

Path("backscatter-graph.xml").write_text(xml)
```

### From functions

The same graphs are available as functions, which suits scripts that work with
XML files. `build_backscatter_graph()`, `build_coherence_graph()` and
`build_interferogram_graph()` return the XML for a settings object, and
`xml_to_mermaid()` turns any graph XML into a diagram, including one saved
earlier:

```{python}
from s1bursts import CoherenceConfig
from s1bursts.snap_graph import build_coherence_graph, xml_to_mermaid

xml = build_coherence_graph(CoherenceConfig())
diagram = xml_to_mermaid(xml)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(f"```{{mermaid}}\n{diagram.replace('flowchart LR', 'flowchart TD')}\n```")
```

### For your SNAP version

The coherence and interferogram graphs differ slightly between SNAP 13 and 14.
Without a version, s1bursts builds the graph for SNAP 13. Pass the version of
your installation to see the exact graph that processing will run:

```{.python}
from s1bursts import SNAPConfig

version = SNAPConfig().resolved_snap_version
xml = CoherenceConfig().to_xml(snap_version=version)
```

## Corrections s1bursts applies

s1bursts works around four reported SNAP problems, so you do not need to:

- **External DEMs are read half a pixel off.** `prepare_dem_for_snap()` shifts
  the DEM to compensate for this
  [problem](https://forum.step.esa.int/t/external-dem-is-sampled-half-a-pixel-off/46042),
  but only for SNAP versions before the 14.0.2 update, which fixed it.
- **DEM heights use the wrong sea-level model.** SNAP knows only the EGM96 model,
  [even for DEMs](https://forum.step.esa.int/t/copernicus-dem-built-in-path-applies-egm96-while-the-data-is-egm2008/46041)
  based on another. `prepare_dem_for_snap()` converts external DEM heights
  itself; see [Using an external DEM](external-dems.qmd). The built-in
  Copernicus DEM is affected too. To avoid it, download the Copernicus DEM and
  prepare it as an external DEM with `source_crs="EPSG:4326+3855"`.
- **Burst edges come out too dark.** SNAP 13 mixes the empty border of the
  input into the edge pixels during terrain correction, which leaves dark seams
  along the burst edges
  ([forum report](https://forum.step.esa.int/t/sentinel-1-slc-terrain-correction-operator-uses-zero-values-in-interpolation-instead-of-treating-them-as-no-data/45336)).
  s1bursts marks that border as missing before terrain correction. SNAP 14
  fixed the problem, so this matters only for SNAP 13.
- **Areas without DEM coverage become zeros.** Where the DEM has no data, for
  example over the sea at the edge of a burst, SNAP can write zeros instead of
  missing values. s1bursts turns these into `NaN`.

## SNAP versions

s1bursts works with SNAP 13 and 14. It reads the installed version and adapts
the graphs to it, so the same code runs on either. The version is recorded in
every product's `PROCESSING_SOFTWARE_VERSION` tag.

::: {.callout-note}
## Keep one SNAP version per study

SNAP versions give slightly different results for the same burst, so a time
series that switches version contains an artificial step. Between SNAP 13 and
14, backscatter differs by about 0.05 dB and coherence by about 0.004.
:::

SNAP 14 also adds two coherence options, exposed as
`CoherenceConfig.correct_coherence_bias` and `remove_local_phase_ramp`. Both
are off by default, and enabling either under SNAP 13 raises an error.

## Validation

s1bursts products are checked against products of the same bursts from
independent processors. Backscatter is compared with
[OPERA RTC-S1](https://hyp3-docs.asf.alaska.edu/guides/opera_rtc_product_guide/)
from NASA/JPL, and coherence with
[ASF HyP3](https://hyp3-docs.asf.alaska.edu/guides/burst_insar_product_guide)
burst InSAR products. Both use the same Copernicus DEM, so the comparison tests
the processing itself.

Backscatter agrees with OPERA within 0.07 dB over whole scenes. Over very dark
surfaces, near the instrument's noise level, s1bursts reads lower, because
OPERA sets negative values to zero before averaging. HyP3 estimates coherence
with a different method and reads about 0.18 higher at the median, so coherence
thresholds from one product do not transfer to the other.
